newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.S. missiles boost Saddam's standing-diplomats.
newsitem.headline: U.S. missiles boost Saddam's standing-diplomats.

text.p: The U.S. retaliation for Iraq's military incursion into Kurdish areas has strengthened President Saddam Hussein at home, diplomats and analysts in the Iraqi capital said on Friday.

They also said the U.S. missile raids gained Saddam some sympathy and support on both Arab and international levels that could help divide the U.S.-led coalition that ended Iraq's seven-month occupation of Kuwait in 1991.

"The Iraqi tanks and armour push into the Kurdish north to back a main Kurdish group to capture Arbil from rivals. America responds by attacking targets in southern Iraq and expanding the area closed to Iraqi aircraft in the south. It does not sound logical for me," said a U.N. official administering aid to Kurds in northern Iraq.
The 44 U.S. missiles fired at air defence targets in southern Iraq have not changed the new political and military reality emerging in Iraqi Kurdistan in the aftermath of Iraq's assault on Arbil.

Iraqi forces helped Massoud Barzani, head of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), oust guerrillas of arch enemy Jalal Talabani, head of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK). Talabani is now based in the stronghold of Sulaimaniya.

"Barzani asked Baghdad's help out of frustration with U.S. policy towards Iraqi Kurds. Things were deteriorating quickly in the area and there was nothing on the horizon that the U.S. and allies were ready to help Kurds out of their quaqmire," said one diplomat.

For ordinary Iraqis, Saddam emerges as a hero by ignoring U.S. warnings and ordering armoured divisions of Iraq's elite Republican Guards into Kurdish areas -- which Baghdad had not controlled since the 1991 Gulf War -- to capture Arbil for Barzani.
International reaction to the U.S. cruise missile attacks, according to one diplomat, showed Iraqis that many countries were no longer willing to back the tough U.S. policy on Iraq.

"There is international criticism of the attacks. Even a diehard enemy like Syria is not happy...and a powerful (Gulf War) coalition member that is France has withheld its public backing," said the diplomat.

"Clinton's missiles could not change the new picture and the new realities in our Kurdistan. I think it is too late for the U.S. and the West to persuade the Kurds that they can have a future without Baghdad," said a Baghdad University professor, who asked not to be identified.

Travellers and diplomats said Baghdad was slowly removing restrictions on movement of people and trade with Kurdish areas under Barzani's control. One diplomat said Barzani and Baghdad were discussing a pact for an enhanced form of Kurdish autonomy.

"That sure will be an outright victory for President Saddam (Hussein) over Washington. If Kurds accept autonomy from Baghdad and peace and stability returns to northern Iraq it will be very embarrassing for the U.S. to continue its air protection of Kurds," said the professor.
Baghdad traders said the highway to Turkey passing through Barzani's territory was open, with hundreds of Turkish trucks ferrying supplies to Iraq each day.

"I think that Barzani now finds it more to his interests to reconcile with Saddam than making peace with pro-Iran Talabani. Past experience has also taught him that reliance on the West may not bear fruit," said one analyst.

Barzani's family has led the struggle for Iraqi Kurds' autonomy. His father Mulla Mustafa died a fugitive in the United States after the collapse of his movement in 1975 and his brother Idris, who led the struggle for self-rule, also died without seeing his ambitions realised.
Said the Iraqi professor: "For Barzani, the reality on the ground is closer ties with Baghdad."
